newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW - Wharf sees good years ahead.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Wharf sees good years ahead.

text.p: Hong Kong conglomerate Wharf (Holdings) Ltd has gone through two tough years but 1997 will be a gateway to three growth years, executive director John Hung said on Wednesday.

"I am not saying that we will have a very good year in 1997 but it is the beginning of the good times and I really believe that 1998, 1999, 2000 are the three good years," he told Reuters in an interview.
Wharf's investments in telecommunications and cable television were a drag on earnings in 1995 and 1996, he said.
The company posted a drop of 24 percent in 1996 net profit to HK$2.74 billion from HK$3.60 billion the previous year.
"We had an earnings drag during those years because of the investment plus the fact that we met at the same time with a pretty weak property market," said Hung.
"We are glad to say that that is behind us now."
Hung noted that the company had earnings growth of 25.4 percent in 1996. if 1995's results were stripped of a HK$1.51 billion exceptional gain.
"This year I would not dare predict such a growth of 25 percent - if it happened fine. In 1998 there will be growth."
Hung said that costs at Wharf's cable television unit Wharf Cable Ltd had stabilised by the end of 1996 and the trend of subscriber takeup was improving.
Cable was making a net gain of some 12,000 subscribers per month and expected 375,000 subscribers by July 1997, he said. The unit is expected to meet breakeven point at the end of 1997.
Hung said the property market also had seen an improvement after a slump from late March when the Hong Kong government imposed measures to curb speculation.
"I think it was a very short period of panic for a couple of months and now it has come back. The market is going again. I have people knocking on my door once more," he said.
"I sincerely believe the market will run up stronger in the later part of this year than now," he added.
Hung said the company was likely to launch its Diamond Hill residential project during the fourth quarter of this year but was closely watching developments in the real estate market.

"It is difficult to say how much we will put on the market because of the recent rule that came out from the government which said if you sell one apartment you have got to sell the project within six months," said Hung.

"We have got five huge blocks at Diamond Hill to put out and the thought is to start marketing it in the last quarter. We have to see that the market is able to sustain itself before we put the first one out because basically you have got to sell the whole lot within six months."

Hung said Wharf's Gateway II development in Kowloon would also start contributing to results in 1998. Wharf projected rental income from the development of HK$315 million in 1998, HK$1.29 billion in 1999 and HK$1.43 billion in 2000.
Shares in the Hong Kong conglomerate have declined this year, closing at HK$32.00 on Wednesday, while the Hang Seng blue chip index has been hitting record highs.

"You can buy in now at this low price and then ride with us over the next several years or you could decide that you will not buy into Wharf until such time that the earnings growth is more imminent," said Hung. "But the chances are that you will have to pay a higher price."
